game-dev-math/part-1-intro-to-math-conce.title: Part 1 - Intro to Math Concepts for Game Design
game-dev-math/part-1-intro-to-math-conce.description:
Because we will be rendering objects and systems into a digital screen, it is useful to understand a bit about Cartesian Coordinate Systems. The name is derived from Renee Descarte, famous french Thinker and Mathematician, and is the groundwork foundation for just about every foundational subject we're going to be talking about with the math going into Game Design. The basics of it is pretty simple. When indicating placement along a line, you can value points as discrete distances from one another. For instance, with the above line, we can say that the distance between 0 and 2 is, in fact, a value of | 2 |. In math terms, this is pretty easy to equate out. You take any two points, A and B, and subtract A from B
This seems awfully rudimentary. Why even bring it up at all? In one dimension, as pictured above, things are easy to parse out. We can look at the line and objectively be able to eyeball the distances that things are spaced apart from each other. If we were to interpolate this line over into the 1000's, we could still use very basic mathematics to determine precise distances between two different points. There's two elements where this gets tricky - when we start to move into multiple dimensions and when we get into more precise calculations using decimal points. When we start to move into a multi-axis Cartesian Units, we're going to have to talk about the way digital screens render out. In your traditional math class, you will have this kind of crossed-axis set up:
Each one of the quadrant represents X and Y values in either ascending or descending values, running along both positive and negative values. Notice how Y behaves as it should naturally, with ascending values corresponding to positive Y values. Digital screens play a little differently
Digital Screens start rendering in the upper left hand corner and then ascend both X to the right and increase Y descending downward. The point where they meet in the upper left is called the origin point and is critically important to understanding how things are not only placed within any given scene, but also how objects are produced. Let's take a look at how this works in practice. Here let's introduce Daryl.
Daryl wants to move to the bottom right corner of the screen. Now, to our eyes, we would naturally need to increase the X value to make him move to the right. That makes sense! But because Daryl is rendered onto a digital screen, we will need to take Daryl's Y position and, instead of subtracting him to move DOWN, we will need to add to his Y value to make him move in the intended direction. It is odd! And almost on purpose. It is important to know how to quantify 2D coordinate positions so that we can communicate with our digital screen where a thing is not only starting, but how to move it to where we need it to go.
For instance, Daryl has an X and Y coordinate that he starts on. This is quantified as: The Dot that he is moving towards always has an (X,Y) position. For argument's sake, let's give each of these objects some arbitrary values:
How far would Daryl have to travel in order to get from his position to the position of the dot? We already know how to do this with 1D math: But how do we calculate this when we have two X and two Y values? We can borrow another formula:

What this formula gives is something pretty far fetched and seems pretty inaccurate. It can give you a good idea of the distance between two differnt points, but a straight line is always going to be faster. Thats where Part 2 -Vectors and 2D Trigonometry comes into play!

game-dev-math/part-2-vectors-and-2d-trig.title: Part 2 -Vectors and 2D Trigonometry
game-dev-math/part-2-vectors-and-2d-trig.description:
So far we have talked mostly about points, which are great for static objects that exist on a screen and aren't going to be doing much. Video games have interactive elements though, and we want to encourage both our systems and our players to be able to move stuff around and interact with things that are moving around! That is where Vectors come in. As discussed, we can interpret the position of any object in 2D space using X and Y coordinates A vector also receives similar X and Y components, but **magnitude**. Magnitude refers to the direction of the vector, giving it an implied length. Let's take a look at a concrete example with this graphWhat we have here are two distinct points: Point A and Point BWe need to figure out two primary components to this vector. The first we will call it's displacement.
This is a simple as using the formula from Part 1 - Intro to Math Concepts for Game Design We take the two points and subtract the target point's components from the original point's components. Putting them together you'll get a new X and Y coordinate. For the sake of our argument here, let's assume that the result for the vector in our graph is: This represents the relative displacement along the X and Y axes for our two points. This doesn't completely describe the vector though, because we also need to account for its **magnitude**
Drawing in those lines, what we have is in fact, a RIGHT TRIANGLE. That's where basic Trigonometry comes into play. So we have a Vector that is ( 3, 4) and we want to find its magnitude. If you remember your basic Trigonometry rules, what we are looking for is the hypotenuse of our right triangle we have assembled here. In case you need a reminder of what the Pythagorean Formula isLet's plug that into the Vector coordinates we have: With just a few simple steps using some basic Trigonometry, we can surmise that the magnitude of our Vector is 5!
In games, you will want to measure distances between things all the time. You will want to measure the distance between your player and a coin they might collect, or figure out how far a projectile might need to travel. For each one of these calculations, you will need to take the two points - one being origin and the other being destination - and you will have to figure out what that distance is going to have to be. Triangle are great for helping you to figure that out, with a little help from Pythagoras we can solve it.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
